This differs slightly from the \cite{HH13} formulation, where $U$ acts on the all-$\ket{0}$ initial state and $\reg{B}$ is a third output register.
There, when $|\reg R|$ is sufficiently larger than $|\reg{BH}|$,
Page's theorem implies for a typical $U$ that the reduced state on the system $\reg B \reg H$ is nearly maximally mixed and recovery from $\reg R$ is information-theoretically possible \cite{HH13}.
This remains true here: decoupling implies that a recovery map with high fidelity exists ~\cite{DBWR14}.
A decoder with access to both $\reg R$ and $\reg H$, along with inverse access, could simply apply $U^\dagger$ to the original output, recovering the original input qubit with one query.
With access only to $\reg R$ and not $\reg H$, this trivial strategy fails.
We allow queries to $U,U^\dagger,U^*,U^{\mathsf T}$, including their controlled versions, and show that recovery still requires exponentially many queries in the regimes stated below.
The circuit and its initial auxiliary state must be chosen independently of the sampled $U$.

\subsection{Results}
\label{sec:main-results}

We measure recovery by $\mathbb E_{U \sim \mu_n}\bra{\Phi^+} \rho_\reg{BA} \ket{\Phi^+}$, the squared Bell-state fidelity of $\reg{BA}$ averaged over $U$.
Outputting a qubit independent of $\reg R$ gives fidelity $1/4$.
Our lower bounds apply to every constant improvement over this value.

\Needspace{11\baselineskip}
\begin{informaltheorem}
Let $|\reg R|\geq|\reg H|$ and fix $\delta>0$.
Every decoder whose circuit and initial auxiliary state are independent of $U$, and whose Haar-averaged Bell-state fidelity is at least $1/4+\delta$, requires
\[
  \begin{array}{ll}
    \Omega(2^{|\reg H|}) & \text{queries with forward-only access},\\[3pt]
    \Omega\!\left(\min\{2^{|\reg H|},2^{n/16}\}\right) & \text{queries with all four types of access}.
  \end{array}
\]
Both bounds allow controlled queries and arbitrary computation between queries.
The second also allows a query to coherently select among $U,U^\dagger,U^*,U^{\mathsf T}$ and the identity.
\end{informaltheorem}

The two lower bounds scale the same when $|\reg H|\leq n/16$.
Outside this regime, the $2^{n/16}$ cutoff comes from the approximation to the Haar oracle used in the proof.
The formal bounds and their implications are in \cref{thm:all-haar,cor:forward-haar,cor:query-lower-bounds}.
The same lower bounds hold if a fixed decoder succeeds on any constant fraction of Haar oracles, by \cref{cor:typical-decoding}.

We demonstrate the decoding bounds by showing bounds for the easier distinguishing task,
in which an algorithm receives $\reg{BR}$ and access to $U$ and must distinguish the joint state in the real experiment from the maximally mixed state on $\reg{BR}$.
A successful decoder implies a successful distinguisher by acting on $\reg R$ and measuring $\reg{BA}$ onto the $\ket{\Phi^+}$ Bell state.
The test accepts with the decoder's fidelity in the real experiment and with probability $1/4$ in the mixed\footnote{
In similar arguments this is often called the ``ideal'' or ``hybrid'' experiment, especially when it models the desirable behavior of a cryptographic primitive.}
experiment.

We discuss a matching upper bound in \cref{sec:decodability-upper}, where
for $|\reg R|\geq|\reg H|+1$ we specialize the Uhlmann algorithm of Utsumi et al.~\cite[Theorem~13]{UNWT25} with an oracle-independent cutoff to obtain an $O(2^{|\reg H|})$-query decoder using forward and inverse queries, with average fidelity at least $1-2\cdot2^{(|\reg H|-|\reg R|)/2}-\epsilon$ for any fixed $0<\epsilon<1/2$.
For $|\reg H|\leq n/16$ and $|\reg H|\to\infty$, it achieves every fixed target fidelity in $(1/4,1)$.
Hence our lower bound with all four query types is tight in this regime.

We also discuss several applications in \cref{sec:applications}, including a linear rank lower bound for the Uhlmann transformation task
and the security of using the Haar-random oracle to generate EFI pairs and quantum commitments.
An Uhlmann transformation aligns two purifications by acting only on the accessible subsystem.
For inaccessible marginals $\rho,\tau$, the relevant rank is $r=\operatorname{rank}(\sqrt\rho\sqrt\tau)$.
The maximum root overlap is $\|\sqrt\rho\sqrt\tau\|_1$; its square is the maximum squared overlap.
With $|\reg R|=15|\reg H|$, our source and a fixed target give a family requiring $\Omega(r)$ preparation queries,
matching the known $O(r)$ upper bound at fixed positive error.
The lower bound allows squared-fidelity error up to $1/8$ on Haar average and all four query types including coherent selection,
as long as the algorithm is chosen independently of $U$.

Further, the joint state on $\reg{BR}$ and the maximally mixed state form an EFI pair in our public-oracle model:
they are efficiently preparable, statistically far apart, and computationally indistinguishable against algorithms with oracle-independent circuits and advice.
We use the oracle-relative version of the EFI definition~\cite[Definition~3.1]{BCQ23}, averaging the distinguishing gap over the public Haar oracle.
We bound the expected absolute acceptance gap for every such polynomial-query algorithm with all four query types.
The standard EFI construction then also gives a statistically binding bit commitment~\cite[Lemma~4.7]{BCQ23}.
The Haar encoding itself also commits to an arbitrary qubit: the sender sends $\reg R$ and later reveals $\reg H$.
Our comparison proves computational hiding~\cite[Definition~4.3]{GJMZ23}, and decoupling proves statistical swap binding~\cite[Definition~4.2]{GJMZ23}.

\subsubsection{Organization}
\Cref{sec:preliminaries} defines the access model and sets up the experiments,
and \cref{sec:query-bounds} states the query bounds, along with the reduction from decoding to distinguishing.
\Cref{sec:trace-distance-proof-sketch} proves the trace-norm bound between the marginals in the path recording experiments, which is our main technical contribution.
\Cref{sec:applications} presents the decoder, rank lower bound, and cryptographic consequences.
The appendices give the full commutator calculations and application proofs.

\subsection{Related work}
\label{sec:related-work}
\paragraph{Strong random unitaries.}
Schuster et al.~\cite[Theorems~1 and~2]{SMLBH25} define strong unitary designs from Haar in experiments with a bounded number of queries to $U$, $U^\dagger$, $U^*$, and $U^{\mathsf T}$, and strong pseudorandom unitaries (PRUs) by indistinguishability for efficient experiments with these query types. 
At fixed design order and approximation error, their Theorem~1 gives depth $O(\log n)$ with ancillas and $O(\log^2 n)$ without ancillas.
Under their cryptographic assumptions, Theorem~2 gives strong PRUs of depth $O(\log n)$ with ancillas and $\operatorname{poly}(\log n)$ without ancillas. 

Their lower bounds~\cite[Proposition~1]{SMLBH25} concern circuit depth rather than query count.
In Section~5 they observe that a strong design encodes as well as Haar in the Hayden--Preskill experiment because the Yoshida--Kitaev decoder uses $U^*$, and note that this transfer applies only when decoding is efficient from query access to the four variants.

Our bounds show that decoding from the radiation alone is query-hard for Haar under all four query types.
Transfer to a strong design requires its order and access model to cover the complete experiment: a $q$-query decoder and challenge preparation use $q+1$ calls, or $4q+1$ after reducing selected queries to controlled queries.
An output trace-norm approximation error of $\eta$ changes the average Bell-test probability by at most $\eta/2$.
For a strong PRU, indistinguishability transfers computational hardness to efficient decoders within its security budget, without the secret circuit description.

In Section~6 they ask whether strong PRUs enable new cryptographic applications and suggest that ancilla-free constructions of commitments would be stronger evidence that natural dynamics have cryptographic properties. Our direct qubit commitment requires no secret key. The sender applies the public oracle $U$ to the message qubit and $n-1$ qubits initialized to $\ket0$, without additional registers for encoding.
The real EFI state is prepared by applying $U$ to one half of a Bell pair and $n-1$ qubits initialized to $\ket0$; the other half is the reference register $\reg B$. The bit-commitment protocol keeps a purification register for opening; for commitment to $0$, this register is padded so that both opening registers have the same size.

\paragraph{Radiation decoding.}
Kim, Tang, and Preskill~\cite[Definition~6.1]{KTP20} formulate the hypothesis that low-rank radiation is computationally indistinguishable from a maximally mixed state.
Our bounds give a quantitative analogue in the Haar-random oracle model.
The efficient Hayden--Preskill decoder of Yoshida and Kitaev~\cite{YK17} has access to an entangled partner of the initial black hole.
Here the other input qubits start in a known pure state, and no such partner is supplied to the decoder.

Yang and Engelhardt~\cite[Theorem~1]{YE23} study the hardness of learning Haar-random dynamics before a fresh input is supplied.
Their algorithm finishes querying before it receives the input, whereas our decoder receives the radiation before its queries.
Poremba, Ragavan, and Vaikuntanathan~\cite[Theorem~8.4]{PRV24} bound joint recovery of a classical message by two separated observers, each making one forward or inverse query.

\paragraph{Haar oracles and query access.}
Zhandry~\cite{Zha25} argues that unitary-oracle models should allow controlled access to the unitary, its inverse, conjugate, and transpose.
Tang and Wright~\cite[Theorem~1.1]{TW25} remove controlled queries for problems that do not depend on a global phase in the oracle.
Tang, Wright, and Zhandry~\cite[Theorem~1.3]{TWZ25} show that conjugate queries can give an exponential advantage over forward and inverse queries.
Their Theorem~1.7 also gives a commitment secure with forward and inverse access that one conjugate query can break.
Bartusek and Goldin~\cite{BG26} construct reusable unclonable encryption in the Haar-random oracle model with all four query types and prove a unitary reprogramming lemma.
These results motivate proving our decoding and commitment bounds in the stronger access model.

\paragraph{Recording oracles.}
Zhandry~\cite{Zha19} introduced compressed oracles for quantum queries to random functions.
Carolan~\cite{Car25} extends this approach to random permutations, and Carolan and Majenz~\cite{CM26} improve its soundness bound.
For Haar unitaries, Ma and Huang~\cite[Theorems~5 and~8]{MH24} give forward and bidirectional path-recording approximations, and Schuster et al.~\cite[Theorem~10]{SMLBH25} extend them to all four query types.
Grinko and Yoshida~\cite{GY25} give exact compressed oracles for compact-group representations using Clebsch--Gordan transforms, including all four query types.
Foxman et al.~\cite{FLMNW26} give an exact path-recording construction for closed subgroups of the unitary group.
Our proof uses the explicit approximate maps of Ma--Huang and Schuster et al.; the insertion and deletion estimates are proved for those maps.

\paragraph{Uhlmann transformation.}
Bostanci et al.~\cite[Theorem~10.3]{BEMPQY23} relate radiation decoding to Uhlmann transformation.
Utsumi et al.~\cite[Theorem~13 and Corollary~5]{UNWT25} give an $O(r)$ preparation-query upper bound at fixed fidelity error and a cube-root lower bound in the rank of the inaccessible marginals, at sufficiently small error.
They already apply their algorithm to Uhlmann decoders in Theorem~33 and to Haar-based quantum state merging in Theorem~34.
Our upper bound specializes the algorithm with one rank cutoff that works for every $U$.

Lee and Jo~\cite[Theorem~1.1 and Corollary~1.2]{LJ26} prove nearly quadratic sample lower bounds for estimating fidelity to a known rank-$r$ reference.
At sufficiently small fixed error, their lower bound for a maximally mixed reference also holds with purification copies.
Wang~\cite[Theorems~1.7 and~5.18]{Wan26} proves an $\Omega(r/\log^2r)$ query lower bound for fidelity estimation at sufficiently small fixed error.
The transformation-to-estimation reduction in Utsumi et al.~\cite[Proof of Corollary~5]{UNWT25} gives the same lower bound for Uhlmann transformation with forward and inverse preparation queries.
\Cref{app:fidelity-comparison} gives the reduction and checks its hypotheses.
Liu and Wang~\cite[Theorem~3.3 and Corollary~3.4]{LW26} obtain optimal fidelity estimation when one of the two states is pure, without knowing which one.
Our rank lower bound concerns two mixed inaccessible marginals.

Our lower bound is linear, allows squared-fidelity error up to $1/8$, and includes all four query types on a fixed-target Haar family.
The extension of the query-simulation theorem to all four types is left open in~\cite[Footnote~3]{TWZ25}.

\paragraph{Cryptographic consequences.}
Brakerski~\cite[Theorems~4.1 and~5.2]{Bra23} gives reductions between EFI pairs and radiation ensembles satisfying hardness and strong decodability conditions.
Brakerski, Canetti, and Qian~\cite[Lemma~4.7]{BCQ23} construct quantum bit commitments from EFI pairs.
Bostanci et al.~\cite[Theorem~8.10]{BEMPQY23} characterize commitments with strong statistical hiding and strong computational binding through average-case hard Uhlmann instances with almost equal marginals.
Our Uhlmann family has nearly equal inaccessible marginals on $\reg{BH}$ for most Haar oracles, together with the stated Haar-averaged query lower bound for transforming their purifications.
The separate real and mixed challenges on $\reg{BR}$ form a statistically far EFI pair.
This pair gives the computationally hiding, statistically binding bit commitment proved in \cref{cor:bit-commitment}.

\paragraph{Common Haar states and public unitaries.}
Chen, Coladangelo, and Sattath~\cite{CCS24} and Ananth, Gulati, and Lin~\cite{AGL24} study cryptography when parties receive copies of common Haar states.
They obtain pseudorandom states with bounded-copy security and quantum bit commitments in those models.
Goldin and Zhandry~\cite{GZ25} give conditions for lifting common-Haar-state separations to unitary-oracle separations.
Constructions of pseudorandom states and unitaries in quantum and Haar oracle models also appear in~\cite{Kre21,ABGL24,ABGL25,HY24}.
In particular, the forward-and-inverse constructions~\cite{ABGL25,HY24}, combined with the commitment and EFI implications~\cite{GJMZ23,BCQ23}, already give EFI pairs and commitments in that access model.
Here the adversary can query the public unitary used to prepare its challenge, with all four query types.

\paragraph{Entropy and entanglement.}
Bansal et al.~\cite[Theorem~6 and Appendix~M]{BMBKH24} give EFI pairs by tracing out part of a secret-key pseudorandom state ensemble.
Aaronson et al.~\cite{ABF24} construct indistinguishable pure-state ensembles with different entanglement entropies.
Bouland et al.~\cite{BFG24} obtain public-key pseudoentanglement under the Learning with Errors assumption.
Ryzov et al.~\cite{RGLE26} relate operational definitions of pseudoentanglement to EFI pairs.
Our entropy observation concerns mixed $\reg{BR}$ marginals and follows directly from their rank.

\section{Preliminaries}
\label{sec:preliminaries}

\subsection{Notation}

We write $[m]=\{0,\ldots,m-1\}$.
Registers are denoted by sans-serif letters.
For a register $\reg X$, its size $|\reg X|$ is its number of qubits.
We use $\|v\|_2$ for vector norm, $\|X\|$ for operator norm, and $\|X\|_1=\Tr\sqrt{X^\dagger X}$ for trace norm.
Trace distance is $\frac12\|\rho-\sigma\|_1$.
We write $\mathrm F(\rho,\sigma)=\|\sqrt\rho\sqrt\sigma\|_1$ for root fidelity.
For a pure target $\ket\psi$, squared fidelity is $\bra\psi\rho\ket\psi$.
Quantum channels contract trace distance and cannot decrease fidelity~\cite[Corollary~3.40 and Theorem~3.27]{Wat18}.
All logarithms are base two.

\subsection{The two experiments}
\label{sec:experiments}

Let $n\geq1$, $n=|\reg R|+|\reg H|$, and $x_{0,c}=c\,0^{n-1}$ for $c\in\{0,1\}$.
We identify an $n$-qubit output label with a pair $(r,h)\in[2^{|\reg R|}]\times[2^{|\reg H|}]$.
The oracle $U$ is an $n$-qubit unitary sampled from Haar measure.
The real experiment prepares
\begin{equation}
  \ket{\Psi^{\mathrm{real},U}_0}=\frac1{\sqrt2}\sum_{c\in\{0,1\}}\ket c_{\reg B}\bigl(U\ket{x_{0,c}}\bigr)_{\reg{RH}}. \label{eq:initial-real-state-u}
\end{equation}
The resulting challenge on $\reg{BR}$ is
\[
  \rho_{\reg{BR}}^U=\Tr_{\reg{H}}\proj{\Psi^{\mathrm{real},U}_0}.
\]
The distinguishing algorithm receives $\reg{BR}$ and has no access to $\reg H$.
The mixed experiment supplies $\id_{\reg{BR}}/2^{1+|\reg R|}$ instead, with the same oracle $U$.
The algorithm's query count $q$ excludes the one forward query used to prepare the real challenge.
Let $\rho_q^{\mathrm{real},U^?}$ and $\rho_q^{\mathrm{mixed},U^?}$ be its states immediately after the last query, averaged over $U$; for $q=0$, these are the supplied input states, including the auxiliary state.
Every bound also holds after the algorithm's final oracle-independent channel, including its complete computation when $q=0$, by contractivity.

A uniform bit $b$, sampled independently of $U$, selects the real experiment for $b=0$ and the mixed experiment for $b=1$.
A distinguishing algorithm outputs $a$ and has advantage $\Pr[a=b]-1/2$.
A decoder acts only on $\reg R$ and auxiliary registers and outputs a qubit $\reg A$.
Its squared Bell-state fidelity for a fixed oracle and its Haar average are
\[
  \begin{aligned}
    f_{\mathcal D}(U)&=\bra{\Phi^+}(\operatorname{id}_{\reg{B}}\otimes\mathcal D^U)(\rho_{\reg{BR}}^U)\ket{\Phi^+},\\
    f&=\mathbb E_U f_{\mathcal D}(U),\qquad \ket{\Phi^+}=\frac{\ket{00}+\ket{11}}{\sqrt2}.
  \end{aligned}
\]
Thus fidelity in the decoding task is the acceptance probability of the Bell-state test.
Outputting a fixed qubit independently of the radiation gives $f=1/4$.

\subsection{Oracle algorithms}
\label{sec:oracle-algorithms}

Conjugation and transposition are in the computational basis.
The allowed query types are
\[
  U^?\qquad\text{for } ?\in\{1,\dagger,*,\mathsf T\},
\]
with $U^1=U$.
Forward-only access permits $U$; bidirectional access permits $U,U^\dagger$; four-mode access permits every $U^?$.
A controlled query applies one type conditional on a control register; a selected query coherently chooses among the four types and the identity.
\Cref{cor:selected-queries} states its constant-factor cost.

The algorithm has an $n$-qubit query register $\reg Q$ and a workspace $\reg W$.
In the distinguishing experiment, $\reg W$ includes $\reg{BR}$ and the auxiliary registers.
Its initial auxiliary state is supplied in tensor product with the challenge and is independent of $U$ and $b$.
Every operation between queries is independent of the sampled $U$.
The bounds permit nonuniform circuits, arbitrary auxiliary states, and unbounded computation, subject to this independence condition.

For the proof, we purify the auxiliary state with a register independent of $U$ and $b$ and include it in $\reg W$.
Giving the algorithm this register can only help it.
By also storing measurement outcomes and discarded registers in the workspace, we may take all operations between queries to be isometries.
For a fixed sequence of query types, the enlarged algorithm has the form
\[
  A_{q+1}U_qA_q\cdots U_1A_1,\qquad U_i\in\{U,U^\dagger,U^*,U^{\mathsf T}\}.
\]
All $A_i$ are oracle-independent isometries on the algorithm's registers.
Storing measurement outcomes in a control register includes classical choices in the selected-query model; terminated branches select the identity.

\Needspace{11\baselineskip}
\section{Query lower bounds}
\label{sec:query-bounds}

The two experiments are difficult to distinguish with few queries.
The following state bounds quantify this for a fixed sequence of uncontrolled query types.
Their proofs are given in \cref{sec:trace-distance-proof-sketch}.

\begin{theorem}[Four query types]
\label{thm:all-haar}
Let $|\reg R|\geq|\reg H|$ and $q\geq0$.
For every algorithm in the two experiments of \cref{sec:experiments}, with circuit and initial auxiliary state independent of $U$ and a fixed sequence of $q$ uncontrolled queries to $U^?$,
\begin{equation}
  \|\rho_q^{\mathrm{real},U^?}-\rho_q^{\mathrm{mixed},U^?}\|_1\leq\min\left\{2,\ (25+24\sqrt2)\frac q{2^{|\reg H|}}+\frac{36(q+1)^2}{2^{n/8}}\right\}. \label{eq:all-haar-bound}
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}

Forward-only access gives a sharper comparison, depending only on $q/2^{|\reg H|}$.
Write $\rho_q^{j,U}$ for the same Haar-averaged output when every query is forward, for $j\in\{\mathrm{real},\mathrm{mixed}\}$.

\begin{corollary}[Forward-only bound]
\label{cor:forward-haar}
Under the same independence assumptions as \cref{thm:all-haar}, for $|\reg R|\geq|\reg H|$ and any $q\geq0$, forward-only queries satisfy
\begin{equation}
  \|\rho_q^{\mathrm{real},U}-\rho_q^{\mathrm{mixed},U}\|_1\leq\min\left\{2,\ (12+3\sqrt2)\frac q{2^{|\reg H|}}\right\}. \label{eq:forward-haar-bound}
\end{equation}
\end{corollary}

Both statements compare the complete experiments, in which the challenge and later queries use the same sampled oracle.
We now include controlled and selected queries and derive the distinguishing and decoding lower bounds.

\subsection{Controlled and selected queries}
\label{sec:controlled}

\begin{corollary}[Controlled queries]
\label{cor:controlled-queries}
The Haar bounds in \cref{eq:all-haar-bound,eq:forward-haar-bound} also hold for controlled queries, with the same query count.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}[Proof Sketch]
Tang--Wright~\cite[Theorem~1.1 and Claim~2.6]{TW25} replace each controlled query by one uncontrolled query of the same type.
The replacement circuit is independent of $U$ and its input.
For every fixed $U$ and input, including reference registers, its output is the original output averaged over one common random global phase of $U$.
The real challenge is unchanged under $U\mapsto e^{i\theta}U$, since its preparation acquires only a global phase; the mixed challenge is also unchanged.
Thus the same replacement applies to either challenge, including the oracle-dependent real input.
Haar measure is phase invariant, so both averaged output states and the query count are preserved.
The uncontrolled bounds therefore apply with the same query count.
\Cref{app:controlled-proof} gives the counter construction and the phase-invariance calculation.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Selected queries]
\label{cor:selected-queries}
For $q$ queries coherently selecting among $\id,U,U^\dagger,U^*,U^{\mathsf T}$, \cref{eq:all-haar-bound} holds with $q$ replaced by $4q$.
This includes adaptive choices of query type.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Let $P_0,\ldots,P_4$ be fixed pairwise orthogonal control projectors with sum $\id$.
Set $U_1=U,U_2=U^\dagger,U_3=U^*,U_4=U^{\mathsf T}$.
Then
\[
  \id\otimes P_0+\sum_{j=1}^4U_j\otimes P_j=\prod_{j=1}^4\bigl(\id\otimes(\id-P_j)+U_j\otimes P_j\bigr).
\]
On the range of $P_j$ for $1\leq j\leq4$, only the $j$th factor is nontrivial; on the range of $P_0$, all factors are the identity.
For each fixed projector $P_j$, we can compute its binary control into an auxiliary qubit, make the controlled query, and uncompute the qubit using oracle-independent gates.
Thus four controlled queries implement the selected query.
The claim follows from \cref{cor:controlled-queries}.
Measurement outcomes can be stored in the control, and terminated branches select the identity.
\end{proof}

\Needspace{10\baselineskip}
\subsection{Distinguishing and decoding}

\begin{corollary}[Distinguishing and decoding]
\label{cor:query-lower-bounds}
For $|\reg R|\geq|\reg H|$, a fixed positive Haar-averaged distinguishing advantage requires
\[
  \begin{aligned}
    q&=\Omega(2^{|\reg H|})&&\text{with forward-only access},\\
    q&=\Omega\!\left(\min\{2^{|\reg H|},2^{n/16}\}\right)&&\text{with all four query types}.
  \end{aligned}
\]
Both bounds allow controlled queries; the second also allows selected inverse, conjugate, and transpose queries.
The same bounds hold for a fixed positive decoding fidelity advantage over $1/4$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Let $0\leq M\leq\id$ be the effect for guessing the real experiment and write $\Delta=\rho_q^{\mathrm{real},U^?}-\rho_q^{\mathrm{mixed},U^?}$.
Since $\Tr\Delta=0$, its positive and negative parts each have trace $\|\Delta\|_1/2$.
Consequently,
\[
  \Pr[a=b]-\frac12=\frac12\Tr[M\Delta]\leq\frac14\|\Delta\|_1.
\]
The state bounds give the query lower bounds for any fixed advantage, using $q+1\leq2q$ for $q\geq1$.
At $q=0$, Haar twirling gives equal averaged inputs.
\Cref{app:query-lower-bounds} gives explicit lower-bound constants.

For decoding, run the decoder and measure $\reg{BA}$ with the Bell projector.
In the real experiment this accepts with average probability $f$.
For each fixed $U$, the mixed output is $\id_{\reg{B}}/2\otimes\sigma_{\reg{A}}^U$ for a state $\sigma_{\reg{A}}^U$ of trace one.
Since $\Tr_{\reg{B}}\proj{\Phi^+}=\id_{\reg{A}}/2$, its acceptance probability is
\[
  \Tr\left[\proj{\Phi^+}\left(\frac{\id_{\reg{B}}}{2}\otimes\sigma_{\reg{A}}^U\right)\right]=\frac14\Tr\sigma_{\reg{A}}^U=\frac14.
\]
The resulting distinguishing advantage is $(f-1/4)/2$, with the same queries.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Decoding on a constant fraction of oracles]
\label{cor:typical-decoding}
Fix $p,\delta>0$ and let $|\reg R|\geq|\reg H|$.
The asymptotic decoding lower bounds in \cref{cor:query-lower-bounds} also hold for any $q$-query decoder, with circuit and initial auxiliary state independent of $U$, satisfying
\[
  \Pr_U[f_{\mathcal D}(U)\geq1/4+\delta]\geq p.
\]
The lower-bound constants may depend on $p,\delta$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Using fresh challenges and auxiliary states, a distinguisher estimates whether the decoder's Bell-test probability is above or below $1/4$.
It then tests the original challenge and reverses the outcome if the estimated sign is negative.
A constant number of trials, depending only on $p,\delta$, gives a Haar-averaged acceptance gap at least $p\delta/2$.
The total query count is $O(q+1)$, so \cref{cor:query-lower-bounds} applies.
\Cref{app:typical-decoding} proves the sign estimate and checks conditional independence.
\end{proof}

The path-recording constructions of Ma and Huang~\cite{MH24} and Schuster et al.~\cite{SMLBH25} replace Haar queries by explicit maps
$V, \bar V$ so that $U, U^\dagger, U^*, U^\mathsf T$ are replaced by $V, V^\dagger, \bar V, \bar V^\dagger$ respectively.
$\bar V$ is the recording map for conjugate access, rather than the entrywise conjugate of $V$.
These maps store a ``path record'' of queried input/output pairs in inaccessible left and right query registers $\reg{E_L},\reg{E_R}$,
which store relation states $\ket L_\reg{E_L} \ket R_\reg{E_R}$ where each of $L, R$ is a multiset of pairs in $\left[2^n\right]^2$.
The size $|L|$ counts multiplicities, and $\operatorname{num}(L,e)$ is the multiplicity of the pair $e$.
The notation $L\setminus\{e\}$ removes one copy of $e$.
The union $L\cup R$ adds multiplicities, so $|L\cup R|=|L|+|R|$.
Write
\[
  \Img(L)=\{y:(x,y)\in L\text{ for some }x\},\qquad \Dom(L)=\{x:(x,y)\in L\text{ for some }y\}.
\]
The record basis consists of the normalized symmetric relation states of Ma and Huang~\cite[Section~2.1]{MH24},
with $\ket\emptyset$ denoting the empty relation.
For each fixed size, the states indexed by these multisets form an orthonormal basis of the symmetric subspace:
\cref{app:elementary} gives the explicit description.
A forward recording query can create a pair in $\reg{E_L}$ or delete a pair from $\reg{E_R}$; an inverse query reverses these roles.
The maps $A,B$ describe creation with a fresh output or input, and their adjoints describe deletion.
The barred maps exchange the two records, as summarized below.
Our $A,B$ are the maps denoted $V^L,V^R$ in Ma--Huang~\cite[Definition~25]{MH24}; $\bar A,\bar B$ correspond to the barred maps in Schuster et al.~\cite[Definition~25]{SMLBH25}.
For $|L\cup R|<2^n$, the two parts of the bidirectional oracle of Ma--Huang~\cite[Definition~25]{MH24} are
\begin{align}
  A\ket x_\reg Q\ket L_\reg{E_L}\ket R_\reg{E_R}&=\frac1{\sqrt{2^n-|\Img(L\cup R)|}}\sum_{y\notin\Img(L\cup R)}\ket y_\reg Q\ket{L\cup\{(x,y)\}}_\reg{E_L}\ket R_\reg{E_R},\nonumber\\
  B\ket y_\reg Q\ket L_\reg{E_L}\ket R_\reg{E_R}&=\frac1{\sqrt{2^n-|\Dom(L\cup R)|}}\sum_{x\notin\Dom(L\cup R)}\ket x_\reg Q\ket L_\reg{E_L}\ket{R\cup\{(x,y)\}}_\reg{E_R}. \nonumber
\end{align}
The corresponding creation maps for conjugate access are those of Schuster et al.~\cite[Definition~25]{SMLBH25}.
They have the same fresh-coordinate rule, with the destination records exchanged:
\begin{equation*}
  \bar A=\operatorname{SWAP}_{\reg{E_LE_R}}A\operatorname{SWAP}_{\reg{E_LE_R}},\qquad \bar B=\operatorname{SWAP}_{\reg{E_LE_R}}B\operatorname{SWAP}_{\reg{E_LE_R}}.
\end{equation*}
Each map is zero outside its defining domain. The path recording oracle is then
\begin{align}
  V&=A(\id-BB^\dagger)+(\id-AA^\dagger)B^\dagger,\nonumber\\
  \bar V&=\bar A(\id-\bar B\bar B^\dagger)+(\id-\bar A\bar A^\dagger)\bar B^\dagger, \nonumber
\end{align}
so that $V, V^\dagger, \bar V, \bar V^\dagger$ replace $U, U^\dagger, U^*, U^\mathsf T$, respectively.
The projection factors keep the $A$ and $B$ terms separate, so that $V$ and $\bar V$ are both partial isometries.
Each increases $|L \cup R|$ by at most one.

\cite{SMLBH25} show that this replacement results in approximation error of at most $O \left( \frac{q^2}{2^{n/8}} \right)$
in trace distance between the output state using Haar queries and the one using path recording queries.
For forward only queries, this is instead $O \left( \frac{q^2}{2^n} \right)$~\cite{MH24}.
Their approximation theorems apply to a complete circuit starting with empty records, including the one call that prepares the real challenge.

In general $c\in\{0,1\}$, $r\in[2^{|\reg R|}]$, $h\in[2^{|\reg H|}]$, and $x,y\in[2^n]$.
The initial path-recording purifications are
\begin{align}
  \ket{\Psi^{\mathrm{real},V^?}_0}&=\frac1{\sqrt{2^{n+1}}}\sum_{c,r,h}\ket{c,r}_{\reg{BR}}\ket h_{\reg{H}}\ket{\{e_0\}}_{\reg{E_L}}\ket\emptyset_{\reg{E_R}}, \label{eq:initial-real-purification}\\
  \ket{\Psi^{\mathrm{mixed},V^?}_0}&=\frac1{\sqrt{2^{n+1}}}\sum_{c,r,h}\ket{c,r}_{\reg{BR}}\ket h_{\reg{H}}\ket{e_0}_{\reg{E_0}}\ket\emptyset_{\reg{E_L}}\ket\emptyset_{\reg{E_R}}. \label{eq:initial-mixed-purification}
\end{align}
The first state is obtained by one $V$ query with empty records: $B^\dagger$ annihilates that input, so $V$ agrees with $A$ there.
Tracing out $\reg{HE_0}$ in the second state gives the mixed challenge $\id_{\reg{BR}}/2^{1+|\reg R|}$.
These differ only by the location of the challenge pair $e_0$, and to relate them
we use an insertion map $J$ following the merge-map method of Ananth et al.~\cite[Section~2.1]{ABGL25},
acting only on the external registers $\reg{E_0E_L}$:
\begin{equation}
  J\ket e_{\reg{E_0}}\ket L_{\reg{E_L}}\ket R_{\reg{E_R}}=\sqrt{\operatorname{num}(L,e)+1}\ket{L\cup\{e\}}_{\reg{E_L}}\ket R_{\reg{E_R}}. \label{eq:insertion-map-behavior}
\end{equation}
Note that it is not an isometry:
different choices of $\ket{e_0}_\reg{E_0} \ket L_\reg{E_L}$ can yield the same $\ket{L \cup \{e_0\}}_\reg{E_L}$ after insertion,
so insertion need not preserve inner products.
It aligns the initial states exactly: $J\ket{\Psi^{\mathrm{mixed},V^?}_0} = \ket{\Psi^{\mathrm{real},V^?}_0}$.
For $|L| = \ell$, symmetrizing the inserted challenge with the $\ell$ other positions gives $J = \sqrt{\ell + 1} \Pi_\text{sym}$,
which for the normalized relation states already symmetric on $\reg{E_L}$ gives the coefficient in \cref{eq:insertion-map-behavior}.
Since the symmetrization projection squares to itself, this gives
\begin{equation}
  J^\dagger J =\id+\Sigma,\qquad \Sigma=\sum_{i=1}^{\ell}\operatorname{SWAP}_{0i}, \label{eq:jdj-is-id-plus-sigma}
\end{equation}
where position $0$ is $\reg{E_0}$ and positions $1,\ldots,\ell$ form $\reg{E_L}$.
This is again spelled out in \cref{app:elementary}.
After $q$ queries, the two purifications are
\[
  \ket{\Psi_q^{j,V^?}}=V_qA_q\cdots V_1A_1\ket{\Psi_0^{j,V^?}},\qquad j\in\{\mathrm{real},\mathrm{mixed}\},
\]
with marginals on $\reg{QW}$ denoted by $\rho_q^{j,V^?}$.
Each recording query acts on $\reg Q\reg{E_L}\reg{E_R}$ while the algorithm gates act on $\reg{QW}$.
In the mixed experiment, $\reg{E_0}$ therefore remains isolated throughout the experiment.

Write $\mathcal A$ for the recording-algorithm operator, distinguishing it from primitive creation $A$, and let $\ket\psi$ be the mixed initial vector in \cref{eq:initial-mixed-purification}.
Insertion consumes $\reg{E_0}$, so the real and mixed marginals use different partial traces:
\[
  \begin{aligned}
    \rho_q^{\mathrm{real},V^?}&=\Tr_{\reg{HE_LE_R}}\proj{\mathcal A J\psi},\\
    \rho_q^{\mathrm{mixed},V^?}&=\Tr_{\reg{HE_0E_LE_R}}\proj{\mathcal A\psi},\\
    \widetilde\rho_q&=\Tr_{\reg{HE_LE_R}}\proj{J\mathcal A\psi}.
  \end{aligned}
\]
We bound the difference between the mixed marginal and $\widetilde\rho_q$, and then between $\widetilde\rho_q$ and the real marginal.
Both bounds apply to the full coherent states, grouping contributions with identical final labels.

Both error estimates use the same property of the mixed purification:
its challenge pair stays in $\reg{E_0}$, which neither the algorithm nor the recording maps touch.
Changing $h$ thus changes only the labels in $\reg H,\reg{E_0}$; the coefficient vectors on the algorithm and oracle records are unchanged.
For the mixed state immediately before query $t$, write
\[
  \ket{\phi'_t}=A_tV_{t-1}A_{t-1}\cdots V_1A_1\ket{\Psi_0^{\mathrm{mixed},V^?}}.
\]
The coefficient vectors at every stage can be grouped as
\[
  \ket{\alpha_{c,r}}=\sum_{\substack{x,L,R\\|L\cup R|\leq q}}\ket x_{\reg{Q}}\ket{\alpha_{c,r,x,L,R}}_{\reg W}\ket L_{\reg{E_L}}\ket R_{\reg{E_R}}.
\]
They are independent of $h$, and the mixed-experiment vector has the form
\begin{equation}
  \ket\phi=\frac1{\sqrt{2^{n+1}}}\sum_{c,r,h}\ket{\alpha_{c,r}}_{\reg{QWE_LE_R}}\ket h_{\reg{H}}\ket{e_0}_{\reg{E_0}}. \label{eq:mixed-experiment-state-family}
\end{equation}
The records start empty and each query adds at most one pair, giving the size bound.
The vector has norm at most one because all algorithm gates and query maps are contractions.
Each coefficient includes the sum of all contributions with the same $x,L,R$; no orthogonality of query histories is assumed.

Different values of $(c,r,h)$ give orthogonal labels in $\reg{E_0}$, even when the corresponding workspace vectors overlap.
The normalization in \cref{eq:mixed-experiment-state-family} therefore gives $\|\phi\|_2^2=2^{|\reg H|-(n+1)}\sum_{c,r}\|\alpha_{c,r}\|_2^2$.
Using $n=|\reg R|+|\reg H|$ and the orthogonality of the query and relation bases, we obtain
\begin{equation}
  \sum_{c,r,x,L,R}\|\alpha_{c,r,x,L,R}\|_2^2=\sum_{c,r}\|\alpha_{c,r}\|_2^2=2^{1+|\reg R|}\|\phi\|_2^2. \label{eq:coefficient-energy}
\end{equation}
For fixed $r$, the labels $(r,h)$ are distinct query labels, so also
\begin{equation}
  \sum_{c,r,h,L,R}\|\alpha_{c,r,(r,h),L,R}\|_2^2\leq\sum_{c,r,x,L,R}\|\alpha_{c,r,x,L,R}\|_2^2=2^{1+|\reg R|}\|\phi\|_2^2. \label{eq:diagonal-energy}
\end{equation}
The first identity will bound the marginal error by counting recorded pairs.
The second will bound deletion of the challenge pair, for which the query must equal $(r,h)$.

\subsubsection{The error due to $J$ not being an isometry}
In the first case, the error comes from insertion ``forgetting'' which pair in the record $\ket{L \cup \{e_0\}}_\reg{E_L}$ was the challenge,
causing more than one query history to contribute to a branch's norm.
For a vector $\ket\phi$ arising in the mixed experiment, define
\[
  K_\phi=\Tr_{\reg{HE_0E_LE_R}}[\Sigma\proj\phi].
\]
Because $J$ acts only on the traced out environment, using \cref{eq:jdj-is-id-plus-sigma} gives
\begin{equation}
  \Tr_{\reg{HE_LE_R}}[J\proj\phi J^\dagger]=\Tr_{\reg{HE_0E_LE_R}}[\proj\phi]+K_\phi. \label{eq:marginal-identity}
\end{equation}
Consequently, the desired comparison splits as
\begin{equation}
  \rho_q^{\mathrm{real},V^?}-\rho_q^{\mathrm{mixed},V^?}=\Tr_{\reg{HE_LE_R}}\!\left[\proj{\Psi_q^{\mathrm{real},V^?}}-J\proj{\Psi_q^{\mathrm{mixed},V^?}}J^\dagger\right]+K_{\Psi_q^{\mathrm{mixed},V^?}}. \label{eq:comparison-decomposition}
\end{equation}
\begin{lemma}[Marginal error from insertion]
\label{lem:insertion-error}
For every vector $\ket\phi$ of the form in \cref{eq:mixed-experiment-state-family}, with coefficient vectors independent of $h$ and supported on $|L\cup R|\leq q$,
\begin{equation}
  \|K_\phi\|_1\leq\frac q{2^{|\reg H|}}\|\phi\|_2^2,\qquad \|J\phi\|_2^2\leq\left(1+\frac q{2^{|\reg H|}}\right)\|\phi\|_2^2. \label{eq:insertion-error-bound}
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
The proof is in \cref{app:insertion-error-bound-proof}. The bound uses the stronger invariant in \cref{eq:mixed-experiment-state-family}: all mixed-experiment operations leave $\reg{HE_0}$ untouched, so the coefficient vectors are independent of $h$. The proof bounds the crossed coherent terms by counting at most $q$ recorded pairs. Inaccessibility of $\reg H$ alone would not imply the required independence.

This only works because the algorithm has no access to $\ket h_\reg H$,
meaning that its choice of which query paths to put weight on must remain uncorrelated with $h$.

\subsubsection{The error due to $J$ not commuting with the algorithm}
In the second case, our goal is to show that $J$ ``almost commutes'' with the algorithm for this particular initial state,
in the sense that the difference between the algorithm's reduced states under the two orders is small in trace norm.
$J$ commutes exactly with any non-query algorithm operations, as those cannot touch the external registers, so the work is to bound its commutator with the algorithm's queries.
We use a hybrid argument, bounding the commutator of $V^?$ and $J$ for just one query (on relevant intermediate states in the mixed experiment),
and then use the triangle inequality to conclude a bound after all $q$ queries.

title: Energy-constrained two-way capacity bounds for noisy Gaussian channels
abstract: A gap between achievable rates and converse bounds persists for energy-constrained bosonic communication in the presence of excess noise. We derive a unified adaptive weak-converse bound for thermal attenuation, noisy amplification, and additive Gaussian noise under an unconditional mean transmitted-photon-number constraint. The bound applies to arbitrary adaptive protocols with quantum memories and constrains the two-way quantum, entanglement-distribution, private, and secret-key capacities. It vanishes throughout the entanglement-breaking region and approaches the corresponding PLOB bound at infinite energy. At finite energy, it improves the evaluated Gaussian squashed-entanglement and PLOB bounds in relevant parameter regimes, while comparison with hashing rates quantifies the remaining gap to achievability. The result provides a common energy-dependent benchmark for noisy bosonic Gaussian channels and extends finite-energy converse methods beyond the quantum-limited setting.
summary:
**TL;DR** This paper derives a single closed-form, energy-dependent weak-converse function 𝓕_{τ,v}(N) that upper bounds the two-way quantum, entanglement-distribution, private and secret-key capacities of thermal-loss, noisy-amplifier, and additive-noise bosonic channels under an unconditional mean transmitted-photon constraint. The bound vanishes exactly on the entanglement-breaking boundary (v ≥ τ), recovers PLOB as N → ∞, and at N = 1 beats the best previous (minimum of Gaussian squashed-entanglement and PLOB) bounds by 31–41% in the worked examples.

**The big picture** Fundamental limits on quantum communication and key distribution over optical channels are usually stated assuming unlimited transmitter power, but real senders have an energy budget, and the known finite-energy upper limits are loose once the channel adds excess noise. This work extends a channel-simulation technique — replacing each channel use by a fixed entangled resource consumed by local operations and classical communication — from the idealized noiseless-environment case to genuinely noisy channels, and evaluates the entanglement of the resulting noisy resource exactly. The payoff is a single formula that interpolates between zero capacity for very noisy channels and the known infinite-energy limits, tightening the benchmark against which practical repeaterless protocols are judged.

**Key contributions**
- A unified converse function covering all three phase-insensitive noisy Gaussian families, valid for arbitrary adaptive protocols with unbounded quantum memories and two-way classical communication.
- Exact evaluation of the relative entropy of entanglement of the mixed photon-sector resource states, with proof that a condensate-twirl separable state is the optimal comparison, plus product additivity on finite tensor products.
- Operational proof of concavity/monotonicity of the bound (not read off the formula), enabling averaging over per-use energies x_i.
- An exact integral identity for the residual gap to the hashing rate: 𝓕 − I_hash = ∫_t^{min(N,y)} log₂[(L−z)/z] dz > 0.
- Finite-error rate bounds: (1−ε)log₂d ≤ Σ𝓕(x_i)+h₂(ε) and (1−e)²log₂d ≤ Σ𝓕(x_i)+h₂(2e−e²).

**How it works** The channel is factored as 𝓛_a followed by 𝓐_{G,0}; its action on a maximally entangled state within a fixed total-photon-number sector defines the resource J_{s,m}. A ladder operator C_± = Σ r_i b_i block-diagonalizes the conditional states, giving explicit eigenvalues H_h(z) with z = τ/[(1+v−τ)v] > 1 exactly in the non-entanglement-breaking region. Concentration of the sector labels (K/s → y, H/s → t, the smaller root of t(L−t) = τN(N+1)) yields the per-mode entanglement density 𝓕. A block inequality using phase-covariant pinching costs only g(s(τx+v)) = o(s); a replica argument over independent copies of a single fixed input eliminates that overhead, and telescoping along the protocol plus concavity converts per-use energies into the budget N.

**Why it matters** It supplies a common, physically meaningful finite-energy benchmark for repeaterless CV-QKD and quantum communication over thermal and amplifier channels — the regimes actually relevant to free-space and satellite links — and demonstrates that keeping the energy constraint inside the simulation resource converts otherwise energy-blind entanglement bounds into sharp converses.

**Caveats** This is a weak converse only; the author explicitly notes that public vacuum dilution under an unconditional mean-energy constraint blocks inferring a strong converse, and exact strong-converse thresholds remain open. A quantitative gap to achievability persists (e.g. 0.24 vs 0.37 bits for the thermal-loss example), and hashing is not claimed optimal. The proof is modular on a companion work's simulation, truncation, and privacy-test machinery. No finite-blocklength refinement, and only unconditional mean-photon-number constraints are treated.
